---
title: "Studyflow"
description: "A visual notation for experimental research"
---

Studyflow is a coordination notation for experimental research in cognitive sciences and adjacent fields, based on BPMN 2.0. Your tools compute; Studyflow coordinates them.

![A training experiment written as one studyflow file.](assets/img/studyflow_example_1.svg){#fig-studyflow fig-alt="A left-to-right diagram. A plain circle labelled Start leads through Study Instruction, BIG-5, 2-Back (pre-test), and Useful Field of View. A diamond then splits the path three ways -- the branches labelled AVGP, Control, and NVGP -- into Action Video Game, Tetris, and No Game (Rest). All three rejoin at 2-Back (post-test), then Debrief, then a heavy-outlined circle labelled End."}

## The gap

A study is written down once for each audience — a protocol, a preregistration, a script, a notebook, a figure — and nothing checks the copies against each other. They drift. Solution attempts have focused on the *data* — standardizing its shape, its storage, and its metadata — but the *process* that produced it is still scattered across prose, slides, and glue code.

## Computation and coordination

A complete programming model has a **computation model** and a **coordination model** — the part that binds individual activities into an ensemble[^gelernter]. Ordinary code has a first-class notation for the first and none for the second: ordering, dependencies, and what each stage hands the next end up spread through call graphs and shared state.

That is exactly where a study's drift accumulates, because coordination is also the half that gets described to an ethics board, registered, drawn for a paper, and rebuilt by a replicator — four accounts of something the code never states in one place. Studyflow externalizes it: computations stay in the tools built for them, and the notation carries the coordination.

## One file, many readings

| The same file is | Serving |
|:--|:--|
| a protocol | a colleague, a reviewer, an ethics board |
| a runnable study | participants, or a model in the participant's seat |
| an analysis specification | the pipeline that ran, not a description of it |
| a figure | the Methods section of a paper |

Each is a [projection](specification.qmd#projections) of one object, so there is no second copy to fall out of step.

## Why extend BPMN

Studyflow does not invent a notation. It extends [BPMN 2.0](https://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/2.0/), standardized as ISO/IEC 19510, inheriting a control-flow vocabulary with defined semantics, a serialization fixed by a standard body rather than a vendor, and an extension mechanism that keeps a file readable by generic BPMN tools. Two decisions hold the cost down for a researcher who does not know BPMN: an author works in domain terms, and execution semantics come from this specification rather than a third-party process engine.

| Neighbouring tool | What it owns | What Studyflow adds |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Experiment builders and task scripts | the trial, the stimulus, the runtime | the consent, eligibility, allocation, and data flow around them |
| Workflow engines | executing computation graphs at scale | a study's cycles, interrupts, and human steps, and a definition a reviewer can read |
| Data standards | the shape of what was collected | the process that produced it, referenced to those standards |
| Provenance standards | a record of what ran | a plan written in advance, in the same object as its record |
| Reporting guidelines | which items must be reported | the items attached to the steps they describe |

It replaces none of them. [Specification](specification.qmd) defines the object, its projections, and its execution semantics; [Reference](reference.qmd) catalogues what ships.

[^hardwicke]: Hardwicke, T. E., et al. (2018). Data availability, reusability, and analytic reproducibility. *Royal Society Open Science*, 5(8), 180448.

[^variability]: Botvinik-Nezer, R., et al. (2020). Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams. *Nature*, 582, 84–88.

[^gelernter]: Gelernter, D., & Carriero, N. (1992). Coordination languages and their significance. *Communications of the ACM*, 35(2), 97–107.
